clean-docs: Write or rewrite any document so a real reader can use it: emails, memos, reports, essays, cover letters, resumes, proposals, meeting minutes, lab reports, study guides, policies, newsletters, READMEs, and technical docs. Fixes the words: one reader and one purpose, a length budget, every fact traced to the sources you gave, no AI filler or padding. Use whenever someone asks to write, draft, rewrite, tighten, summarize, shorten, proofread, or "clean up" a document, says text sounds like AI or is too long, wordy, generic, or padded, or asks for help with their report, paper, essay, email, letter, resume, notes, or README, even if they never name the skill. For layout as a PDF or Google Doc use polished-docs; for a one-page condensed version use cram-sheet.
polished-docs: Lay out any document so it looks right as a PDF and as a Google Doc: real heading styles, one readable font, correct spacing and indents, sane line length, page numbers, nothing stranded at a page bottom, and the right form for the type (business letter, memo, resume, APA or MLA paper, report). Use whenever someone asks to format, lay out, polish, or "make this look professional", "format my paper", "turn this into a PDF", "put this in a Google Doc", or "clean up this Google Doc", or says pasted text shows literal # or **, has stray spacing or typed bullets, or looks different in Docs. Run after clean-docs when the words themselves are padded or generic; use cram-sheet for a one-page condensed version.
cram-sheet: Fit a topic onto one or two readable pages: study sheet, cram sheet, cheat sheet, exam review, one-pager, quick reference, meeting prep sheet, process or policy summary, "the short version", "fit this on one page". Works for any subject (a chapter, a policy, a process, a role, a library). Ranks facts by how often they are needed, cuts instead of shrinking type (8pt floor), reports what was cut, and checks every claim against the material you gave. Use whenever someone wants to review, memorize, or hand off a condensed version of notes, a textbook chapter, a report, a procedure, or code docs, even if they never say "cram sheet".
